utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. And good afternoon, Mr. Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I want to pick up on one matter from yesterday that I interrupted you endeavouring to explain to us. You said to us that in the rules it said that in the war the General Staff becomes the Supreme Command Staff, and you then said: "So in wartime the Supreme Command comprises the president with his advisors and associates, and the Supreme Command Staff is an integral part of the Supreme Command." Can you help me by explaining a little more about the Supreme Command as you understood it and who were the advisors and associates.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have to say that at the time I did not go into all that detail too much, who was by the president as the supreme commander; however, what I remember now are the rules, namely that the Supreme Command is the highest organ that commands the army. In peacetime, it's the Supreme Defence Council; in wartime, it is the supreme commander. So I allow for the possibility that perhaps I'm making - well, let me say this - a mistake. Perhaps I'm not saying things very precisely, but certainly this was a solution that was provided for earlier on in the JNA, and that is what I had in mind as such. So who is by the supreme commander, that is to say the president? I do not rule out the possibility that some changes were introduced and that it was supposed to be the Supreme Defence Council as a whole; however, as far as I know, throughout all this time not a single meeting was held of the Supreme Defence Council. That is what was known publicly. So next to him he had the military cabinet or office. There were a few officers in it in charge of certain matters, and when necessary he could call whoever else he might have needed to use that person as an advisor for a particular matter. So that would be the composition. As for the General Staff, during the war it grows into the Supreme Command Staff. I think I said yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You explained that yesterday that --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that basically it remained the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that it was divided into three parts and -- well, that was the change --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and the basic task was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, let me ask you two things first of all. We know that the presidents of Serbia and Montenegro were part of the Supreme Defence Council. What was their role in the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. President -- we're talking about the state of war, aren't we? As far as I know as a retired general, that is to say as any other citizen, I think that their role was non-existent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just tell me if you actually know anything about the role that they should play during wartime.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you were -- the second thing was this, and you were about to embark on it a moment ago. You said that although the Supreme Command Staff was formed similarly to the General Staff, you indicated that it was perhaps disposed differently, that part of it was in one place where that would not be the case during peacetime. Can you clarify that for me.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that perhaps something happened during the interpretation. First of all, I did not say "perhaps." I said that according to the rules and in practice, as far as I know, when exercises were carried out the General Staff was never in one place, all of them together. Quite simply, so that they could not be jeopardized in any way or targeted, all of them together. So in principle they were subdivided into three parts. One part, along with the chief, was always supposed to be by the supreme commander; the second part was supposed to be at the rear command post, that is to say the remaining part, they are to operationalise through documents, planning, et cetera, everything that is decided upon; and the third part could be deployed at the forward command post depending on what is being done. So basically it was organized in a different way because now the complete administrations were not there any longer. Part of them were along with the basic command post, another part was with the rear command post, and the third part was at the forward command post if there was one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would now ask you to look briefly at the last of the minutes I intend to refer to; that's the 18th of March, P938, and in the English at page 25. Now, in B/C/S that is -- it's page -- well ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be page 23 in the version you have, Mr. Dimitrijevic. It's where General Ojdanic is speaking. It starts with a reference to the theft of pistols. Can you go to the third paragraph, please, of that section where in the middle of the paragraph he refers to the army together with the MUP having to undertake some measures with the purpose of blocking and searching the terrain. And he goes on to say: "I think that we all agree about that, but any other rampage without the knowledge of the army and the corps commanders must be prevented at higher levels ..." Do you know what he was referring to when he talked about any other rampage?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is hard for me now in view of the time distance to be very precise in terms of what he is referring to. However, I believe that all of it can be intimated in relation to what you had asked me about yesterday. There is one thing I wish to say first and foremost; I think it wasn't mentioned yesterday. As far as the method of work of the collegium of the Chief of General Staff is concerned, that is to say all assistants first and foremost would present their assessments, or rather, they would report from their own domains of work; and the chief of the first operative administration talked about engagement and proposals and tasks that are to be carried through subsequently. At the end of each and every collegium --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: May I stop you there, please. We do have a limited amount of time, Mr. Dimitrijevic, and I really want to know if you can recollect what he was referring to by "any other rampage," which doesn't sound like something you would regard as official conduct.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. That's precisely what I wanted to say, that this is the conclusion made by the Chief of General Staff, and he says here in one sentence, the army cannot sit with its arms crossed if a military vehicle had been hit with two officers in it. Yes, he says that before this sentence here, we cannot very well sit idly by if a military vehicle with two officers is hit and just let it pass. There were such cases --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: With respect, Mr. Dimitrijevic, that's not what he's talking about because he's talking about a rampage without the knowledge of the army and the corps commanders and that sort of thing must be prevented at higher levels. Now, that does look like he's talking not about attacks on the army and the MUP but about the activities of the army.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, with all due respect, my understanding of this is his reaction; see, there are killings, woundings taking place, and all this is the result of certain rampages. That's the term he's using. Again, he is expressing practically -- well, I don't want to say that he's complaining, but in a way he seems to be complaining to the collegium that this is happening outside his knowledge and without the army commanders or corps commanders knowing about this if it happens at lower levels. I think that that was the underlying idea of what he had conveyed to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what is it that he's referring to as happening that the superior officers did not know about?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably that the army should be engaged, that units should be used, and that it doesn't go through the General Staff to the army command and to the corps. I assume that that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you understand that to be talking about an action by members of the VJ without authority through proper channels?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that is how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you had occasion to meet with the British military attache. Do you remember also meeting with the British ambassador, Mr. Docherty -- sorry, it's my mistake, Donnelly.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, but as far as I can remember it wasn't one meeting. There were several such meetings at which problems in Kosovo and Metohija were practically the only topic that was discussed and how these problems should be resolved. So the problems were that the verification mission never started operating at full capacity. The problem was, and as a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on a second, please. I want to ask you more direct questions. Are you saying that you met with the British ambassador on a number of occasions?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and always in the presence of the military attache, Mr. Crosland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that was intensely intensive. These meetings took place between November and the end of January/beginning of February because after that, practically, I was outside the main stream, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In one of the communications from that ambassador which has been presented to us, which is P683, there is reference to one of your discussions in which you're recorded as saying that you wished to distance yourself and the Chief of the General Staff, who at that time - this is October - who at that time was General Perisic, from responsibility for recent actions. And it records you as pointing the finger of blame clearly at Sainovic and the MUP and saying that you would be using your best efforts to keep the army out of further entanglement except on the border where they belonged. Is that an accurate reflection of your discussion with Crosland and Donnelly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the first time I see this sheet of paper, and I see that it is a telegram that the military attache, I believe, sent to his headquarters. What I have before me is a summary only, in which it says - that's the second sentence - "dissociates himself and Chief of General Staff from responsibility for recent actions." I don't know what that means, but my understanding is that this is the impression of the person who was writing this, perhaps on the basis of the conversation held or part of the conversation or perhaps some sentences were even misunderstood. Mr. Crosland knew the Serbian language up to a degree. The discussion took place in the liaison officer -- in the liaison office for liaising with foreign representatives, and there was an interpreter present, but if he understood something then there would be no interpretation. And I'm also surprised by this other sentence that he's trying to keep the VJ out of further entanglement. First of all, I was not in a position to do that, and I was not authorised to say any such thing. Probably we talked, and probably like on all other occasions I said that it was my understanding that the army should be at the border primarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, we had a brief technical hitch, Mr. Dimitrijevic. On the second page of this document in paragraph number 6, this is explained more fully where it is said that you conveyed the information that you and the General Staff personnel did not agree with the actions that had been taken in recent months since Sainovic had taken over in Kosovo. Now, what was it that had been happening since he took over that you did not agree with?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, well, to put it this way, that they did not agree with the actions that had been taken since Sainovic had taken over in Kosovo, I never could have said any such thing, and I did not say that because Sainovic absolutely was no authority in Kosovo, and that would have been a lie. He was the chairman of the Federal Commission for cooperation with the verifiers in his capacity as deputy prime minister in charge of foreign affairs. He was there in that capacity down there, but to say that he took over, that he took power, I'm absolutely certain that no such thing could have been said. As for the first part of the sentence, he personally and the General Staff personnel - referring to me - did not agree with the actions -- well, this is a very general statement or conclusion. I did not agree with the information that reached me to the effect that the army was being used beyond the orders given from top all the way down the chain, from the General Staff -- or rather, Supreme Defence Council, General Staff, all the way down to corps level, et cetera. I never agreed to that, and to this day I think that I would not agree to any such thing. Probably I did make comments. Now, it is a matter of free interpretation, his interpretation. On the basis of this, it is my understanding that this is not a recorded conversation, so it's not a recording; this is an interpretation of something that someone could have experienced this way or that way, yes. What it says further on is correct, that I react to this, that due to the humanitarian catastrophe, if it cannot been resolved this way, the bombing would resolve it even less. I kept repeating that to the British and American and all other ambassadors and military attaches. However, that's where we stood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two other points in this document where there is a reflection of your indication that Sainovic was exercising certain power there. Paragraph 8, if you have it, there's a reference to you saying that Sainovic had overridden General Staff wishes. Now, what had he done to override the wishes of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but, Mr. President, if I understand this text correctly, that is Donnelly's interpretation. He asked me, so I really can't say what he based this assertion on. In light of what he said about Sainovic, he probably is referring to what he said in the previous paragraph and so on as to what he thought. So it is an interpretation on the part of Mr. Crosland. That's the way I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, it's very difficult to think of any reason that Crosland and Donnelly would have for recording this inaccurately, and I understand the point you're making about a mistake. But there are several references here to their understanding of you saying that Sainovic was responsible for policy which had changed the way in which the VJ were being used in Kosovo. And what I'd like you to tell us is what he did to alter the way that the VJ were used or what you believed he had done to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm absolutely certain that something along those lines, that Sainovic was the one who changed the military policy. I'm sure that I never said anything of the sort. Sainovic, as I've just explained, was in Kosovo. He had a certain function there. He went, like all the others, to the Pristina Corps command; you asked me about that yesterday. So if Sainovic had been the one to change the policy of the use of the army -- well, that's not something that I said at the time. That's not something that I would be able to say now. I know that at some collegium meetings, in some discussions, I would intervene and say that no civilians - and I think that I specifically mentioned Sainovic's name - could not use the army, could not decide on its use because the chain of command is well-known and it can only be done in accordance with the chain of command. So Sainovic was mentioned in those discussions but as somebody who was there on behalf of the government representing the politicians [as interpreted] of the country there at Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In November, there is another document of a similar nature if you look, please, at P684, and if you look at paragraph 5 of that document. Mr. Petrovic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me, at page 11, line 5 of the transcript, the witness said on behalf of the government where he represented the politics of the country, whereas in the transcript it says "politicians."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you'll see in paragraph 5 that there was a reference to you admitting that the VJ had overstepped the mark during the summer offensive. Can you tell us in what way you understood the VJ to have overstepped the mark?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's the way I phrased it, that it overstepped the mark, first of all, Mr. President, I don't agree with what it says here, that he admitted -- did admit. What does it mean? He was not some kind of a judge that I would be admitting something to. This was probably through the conversation. I'm just noting that in order to give you an idea of how this was interpreted, so I can't really accept that. But I probably did say when he remarked that the army was being used, that there may have been instances of such use and that I deeply disagree with it, and that's nothing new. Because if you allow me, it goes on to say -- there is a comment; it is quite clear that DA saw the army use the heavy artillery and the mortars and so on. So now I'm asking myself, who is DA if I'm General D in the very same passage? I don't think that I can be both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you are. I'm just asking you about the comment that the VJ had overstepped the mark.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Dimitrijevic, it's consistent -- this might be seen to be consistent with things you were saying at the collegium, is it not? I mean, we've been through the collegium minutes, and is this not --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- a repetition of what was being said there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see this as a repetition. I still stand behind this, what I said at the collegium, not in this sense, not to this extent, this is something that I discussed with the military diplomatic representatives with one goal so that they could relay the information, the proper information, to their governments about the situation in the country so that a political solution could be found. Our basic goal - this is what I always insisted on; this is what the General Staff always insisted on - was that a political solution should be found. And if you allow me, the last sentence in this paragraph, paragraph 5, says: "Possibly an attempt to distance the VJ General Staff from the 3rd Army actions under General Pavkovic." So we're talking about October or whatever the time-period. This is the time when Pavkovic was not the commander of the 3rd Army. So I notice quite a few errors here, interpretations that he made, and this doesn't mean that what he saw, what he wrote here, is an accurate depiction of how it really was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you heard of an organization called the MUP Staff for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that it may have been mentioned at the meetings with President Milosevic or at some other meetings to the effect that the MUP had established its staff for Kosovo or in Kosovo in order to exercise control over all the MUP units in Kosovo and Metohija. So I do remember this term being used, the title, the MUP Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did you know --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't know much more about that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know who was at the head of the MUP Staff?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, I don't know that. But according to the chain of command, that would -- should have been General Djordjevic because he was the highest-ranking officer there, but I am not claiming that this was indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you were removed from office on the 23rd of March, were you told why you were being removed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. President Milosevic told me why he relieved me of my office. He said that I had spent a long time in that position, that this was very exhausting work, and that I should get some rest. There was an offer for me to get diplomatic posting, but I refused it. I demanded that I retire because I had all the conditions for it, all the requirements for it, and that's why I retired. So he told me verbatim, Well, you've spent a long time in this position; it's a difficult job; it would be a good thing for you to get some rest. And I said, Mr. President, bombs are about to start falling, and you're offering me to get some rest? Of course, he did not budge, and I refused all the other offers and demanded that I retire; so he accepted and said that I would get a paper confirming that within the next ten days or so, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you consider that his interest in your welfare was the true reason for your -- the termination of your position?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that I had gotten to know President Milosevic quite well, and of course this was just fairytale. The real truth was something else. I personally think that he was under a great deal of pressure - I know that because of the position where I was - to remove me from that post. That pressure came from the MUP, primarily the State Security Service, from General Pavkovic, and probably all that culminated in this decision on his part that one day before the air-strikes began I should be removed from that post and put in retirement. So this story that he served me was a story that I couldn't really credit at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And why did these others want rid of you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably because there were constant complaints about the use of units, the use of the MUP as a whole, the wire-tapping on the part of the State Security Service that I was talking about yesterday. So I think that because I was the way I was, because I always talked straight and didn't mince words, I always told everyone the truth, and I always told the truth to the president, that I was some kind of a problem for those people, and those people wanted to put somebody else on that position, somebody who might be, so to speak, more cooperative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is my understanding correct that on the 4th of February efforts were already underway to remove you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I would be a very bad -- I would be doing a bad job as the chief of the security administration if I had just read in the papers about my removal from office. That was not the case. This initiative to remove me from office started way back in December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In February, General Ojdanic said it was only a proposal and it was up to the president; it was his constitutional right. Who do you understand made the proposal?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no proposals were made on the part of the General Staff; but probably such proposals did reach President Milosevic through informal channels, and it is quite obvious that this particular channel was quite successful in terms of influencing personnel decisions because formally speaking, for somebody to be promoted to the rank of the general or to be removed from an office, transferred somewhere else, or to retire, the proposal should have come from the General Staff, the Chief of the General Staff, with the approval of the defence minister; and then the supreme council would consider this request and decide on it. In this case, this procedure was not followed at all; none of these elements were in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with the exception of the decision on my retirement, which I did receive in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We will confer as a Trial Chamber just briefly, Mr. Dimitrijevic. Just give us a moment while we do that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The course of action we followed in relation to the evidence of Mr. Djakovic was that the Prosecution cross-examined first. We will follow that course today, and at the first break we'll resume -- we'll review the situation so far as time is concerned. Mr. Hannis. You'll now be cross-examined, Mr. Dimitrijevic, by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. I want to, I guess, try to go chronologically for a while, if I may, and I'm going to start with some of the VJ collegium sessions, and I will try not to duplicate questions that you've already been asked by Judge Bonomy. The first one I want to ask you about is Exhibit P921. That's for a meeting on the 19th of June, 1998, and I would like you to go to page 9 in your B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's page 10 of the English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you find that, General, at the very bottom of the page. This is you speaking, and you say: "There is a growing conviction that the MUP does not have the force to combat terrorism. People still cross the border illegally and bring in weapons from Albania. Our units react each day, but it would be naive of us to think that nobody manages to cross over." Do you recall saying that? Wasn't that true? As early as June 1998 there was already a concern about MUP's ability to deal with that problem in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. At that time, there was concern about the ability of the MUP to carry out those tasks. Why? First of all, the MUP had this problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. Let me interrupt you. I have limited time --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To put together a sufficient force and to dispose -- to dispose it to position. So at any rate, there was concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The next thing you said was: "The MUP inter-sector staff has been changed. They are now relocating to Pristina, and MUP General Lukic has been appointed Chief of Staff." Does that refresh your memory about what his position was at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, sir. I don't recall those details, but if that's what it says here, I accept that I did say that and that I had the arguments to back it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go next to a meeting in July. It's Exhibit 3D641. This is from the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the English, Your Honours, we only have two pages. This was a partial translation, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, I need you to look at page 9 and 10 of your copy, the last two paragraphs on page 9. The speaker, I believe, is General Borovic. Did you find the paragraph that starts with a sentence that says: "As concerns certain views according to which we should extend the scope of the army's engagement ..."? You find that? I think it's the second paragraph up from the bottom of page 9.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, excuse me, what is the question? This is what General Ojdanic is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- it's General Borovic, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At page 9, that's General Dragoljub Ojdanic. So first you have Spasoje Smiljanic at the top of the page followed by General Dragoljub Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a typo in my notes. And he is saying: "As far as an anti-terrorist operation is concerned, I'm not aware of such operation, but I would like to stress that since General Dimitrijevic, and we all know that military and diplomatic representatives are now permanently stationed in the area, they will carefully record all developments."

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yeah, I think there's a mistake, Mr. Hannis, on the page that you're referring to. I think you -- I believe you said page 9 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Page 9 of the B/C/S. It's on page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, but this is only a partial English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Right, but for the Court to follow I would think that -- I don't know if the Court can follow this on page 2. Is it -- okay, I just want to make sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm assuming we have on the screen what is going to be asked but maybe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, what should we be looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. You have on the screen the correct English. That second paragraph is where I was beginning: "As concerns certain views ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's what we have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And General Dimitrijevic, can you look at -- on the page 10 for you. You're speaking and you say: "When it comes to the protection of the population in over 200 villages, that part is going on in an organized fashion. As far as the anti-terrorist activities are concerned, they are being carried out, too, taking all these things into consideration. They have been planned so that the MUP forces never appear as initiators but always responding to attacks." That's how it was being done in July 1998, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So if we're talking about the protection of the population, I spoke about that yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that measures were taken to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You answered my question, and I understood you say yes, that's how it was being done, that the MUP forces were never -- it was planned so the MUP forces never appeared as initiators but always responding to the attacks, right? Can you say yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably yes because yesterday I spoke about reacting on several occasions because in all of the reports it always said that a unit had come under an attack, and then there had been a response to that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct. Let me take you to another exhibit. This is P922 for the 20th of July, another VJ collegium meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For you, General, on page 2. And first of all, it's about four lines down. General Perisic is noting that the MUP went to Orahovac the day before, and as you read a few sentences down he says: "And somebody from the army used a combat group ..." Do you see that, first of all? Are you on the same page?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall that discussion at this meeting on July the 20th?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At this point I can't recall -- well, it was ten years ago, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite possible that General Perisic did speak in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you'll go to the next paragraph at the bottom of the paragraph or the bottom half. General Perisic is saying: "I issued an order - I ban the use of the army except in the defence in the border area where it is to act in full compliance with combat ... to protect military facilities and defend army personnel. In any other situation, the decision to use it must be made here ..." And on to the next sentence: "Just refer to that order, why was the army used despite my order, specifically ... find out about the circumstances under which that happened, who violated the order and the proposal ..." Do you recall if that was done, if it was determined who violated General Perisic's order in connection with what happened in Orahovac in July 1998?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as to what happened in Orahovac in July 1998, I really can't comment on that because I don't recall that at all. As regards the second passage in what Perisic is saying on this page, that was how it was; he did issue orders after all the reports that came in that were problematic in terms of the way in which the army was used. He did issue an order that the army could not be used without an order from the General Staff except to protect the state border belt and to protect the facilities in accordance with the rules of combat. But if I am not wrong, yesterday I answered to a question by the Presiding Judge that as a consequence of the failure to comply with this order, the army commander - already General Samardzic, the commander of the 3rd Army - had a disciplinary investigation instituted against General Pavkovic because of the failure to comply with this order. It was in July, and I think that I said yesterday how this investigation ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You did mention that there was some sort of disciplinary proceedings instituted against General Pavkovic. I can't recall precisely what you said yesterday, but I had wanted to follow up and ask you what the outcome of those proceedings were, and do you know what happened?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I mentioned that yesterday as well. Only a few days later, there was a meeting with President Milosevic whereupon he told us that General Pavkovic was being promoted to the rank of lieutenant-general. That was the response to the commander of the 3rd Army and the Chief of the General Staff following their initiative to launch an inquiry, a disciplinary inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, let me remind you --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I mentioned that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, let me remind you of what you're recorded as saying about that yesterday. It came at what was then page 48. I don't have the updated number. This was when you were answering Judge Bonomy's questions about a VJ collegium in December and the discussion about the commander, General Pavkovic, having been in Belgrade for two weeks, et cetera. In that answer you mentioned that: "General Samardzic at some point" -- you said "towards the end of June started disciplinary proceedings to punish Pavkovic because he didn't adhere to orders." Now, this VJ collegium you were just looking at is from the 10th of July. So does that refresh your memory about when the proceedings might have been instituted? Did they happen in June, in which case they must have been for something else other than Orahovac, or did they happen after the 10th of July? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you with a degree of certainty, although I cannot be precise as to the exact date but that it happened in late July, not June, but July. And it was some four to five days later; it may have been on the 28th or the 29th of July, and right after that, a few days later - I believe it was the 4th of August - it was when we were invited to see President Milosevic when, among other things, we were told that General Pavkovic as of that day, in his words, is being promoted to the rank of lieutenant-general. What was mentioned yesterday concerning the December collegium -- well, yes, but that has nothing to do with it. This order, indeed, was issued in July, and on that basis some ten days later, whether on the 28th or the 29th or the 30th, General Samardzic following the order initiated proceedings against General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll see if I can help you out with the dates a little bit because I know this was almost ten years ago. And we have some documents -- I have a document reflecting that General Pavkovic was promoted on the 21st of July, 1998, and 21st of July, 1998, was the same day that you had one of those meetings. General Pavkovic talks about it in his interview with the OTP, and we have other documents reflecting a meeting with President Milosevic on the 21st of July with the highest-level people from the VJ and the MUP, and that's where the plan for combatting terrorism apparently was first presented by General Pavkovic in the presence of Mr. Milosevic. You remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that meeting when he presented the plan, it wasn't there that he was promoted; he was promoted after that. For some reason, the 4th of August is the date that I have in my mind as the date when we attended the meeting with Milosevic, when we learned that Pavkovic was being promoted. Of course, the formal requirements needed to be met subsequently, and there was some time needed to draft a proposal, and I believe the formal appointment came later in late August or in September. But on that day, on that meeting, President Milosevic told us that Pavkovic was promoted that day. I truly cannot recall anything being any different than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, I will tell you we have a document that is a report from, I think, Tanjug. You're familiar with that publication in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And dated the 21st of July, it says: "'Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic has passed a decree on the promotion of Major-General Nebojsa Pavkovic, Pristina Corps commander, to the rank of lieutenant-general,' the military cabinet of the Yugoslav president said on Tuesday, the 21st of July."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I said. Maybe there was a translation -- but it's on the 21st of July, 1998, in Tanjug. If it's published then, would you be willing to concede you might be mistaken about which day and which meeting you learned about this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. Prosecutor. I told you I have no notes or anything that could confirm what I've been telling you. I speak from memory as best as I can recall and as the things happened. Of course, it may have happened ten days before the date I indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, he was promoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I understand. I know it was a long time ago, and you didn't know precisely what you were going to be asked about when you came in. Did you keep any diary or any journals during that time, back in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As all officers, including the generals, I had my workbook. Until the very last day of my professional career I was using it, noting down important things, events, or anything I may have reported or been given a task. All those notebooks were handed over on the 23rd when General Farkas came. As far as I know, they were torn or shredded. In any case, I do not have a single piece of paper relating to that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The notes were the property of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I was doing was in professional terms. That wasn't for private use.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And they were not preserved in the archives, but they were shredded, you say?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And some --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- they were not preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And some VJ witnesses we have had occasionally kept their private notebooks as well. You didn't have anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What would I do with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just to get back to the disciplinary proceedings. You say those were instituted by Samardzic, but when you learned from Mr. Milosevic that Pavkovic had been promoted to lieutenant-general, you understood that those proceedings weren't going any further; is that correct? Or is that just an assumption you made?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Time showed that nothing was done subsequently to, indeed, have those proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know who stopped them or how that was done?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, nothing was done and the procedure was never completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, about that same time, actually, two days later, on the 23rd of July, we have an exhibit, P717. I trust you have a hard copy there. This is a letter written by General Perisic to Mr. Milosevic concerning what General Perisic saw as problems with the use and misuse of the army. Have you ever seen that document before? I think the cover page is just from a book in which this letter was published.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. Prosecutor. I think Perisic showed it to me, but not before sending it but after having sent the letter to President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you'll see that one of the things he complains about in item 1 is the -- what he calls the tendency to use the VJ outside the institutions of the system, and he's suggesting that a state of emergency should be declared. And that was a position that you agreed with at the time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And because you thought for the army to be engaged in fighting the terrorism -- the terrorists, it really needed to be under such circumstances, right, so the army could be fully engaged in Kosovo, not just in the border area and not just regarding VJ property and personnel, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, basically that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Look at --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, I'd like to offer a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please, if you can be brief.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This tallies with what I talked about yesterday. The opinion in the General Staff was something that had to do with what I said yesterday, the surveillance of the Pristina Corps command and the following conversation including President Milosevic. It is then when I said that, I guess you're checking on us because you don't trust us. This is another proof in that regard. Obviously, the army was not being trusted. Obviously, a standing option was to use it little by little and that the state did not want to support such use officially. Because of the escalation of terrorism, they didn't want to declare a state of war. Since they were unable to come up with a political solution, they should have at least come up with a solution on a constitutional use of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If you could look at -- I don't know, it may be page 2 or page 3 for you. It's item number 3, 3(b). This is regarding attempt to command the VJ by unauthorised persons. And do you see where it says: "The attempt by the civilian part of the staff to command the corps ..." Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What staff is that referring to of which there is a civilian part?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you what he had in mind specifically --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you read on --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I do presume, though, that it had to do with persons who were civilians ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, if I may, if you read on, it said: "The corps commander," in this case Pavkovic, "is responsible for assessing the situation and for planning VJ and MUP operations in cooperation with the civilian part of the staff and the MUP for forwarding it to Sainovic and Minic for them to distribute assignments to all except the Pristina Corps ..." So I read that to mean that Sainovic and Minic are engaged in this process, and I'm trying to figure out what staff that has a civilian part is involved in this process. Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I couldn't tell you what staff it was. I don't know what this refers to. As for the other thing, I read it the following way, that Pavkovic as the corps commander was the one that was to assess the situation and make decisions on what needed to be done. Given that Pavkovic could not issue tasks and orders to the MUP, this would mean that some of the civilians, if indeed the situation was like that, was supposed to tell the MUP what they were to do. I'm not familiar with the methodology they used, but that is my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And General, doesn't that say that the civilian part of the staff --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because then Perisic goes on -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Doesn't that suggest that Sainovic and Minic are going to distribute assignments to the MUP and to anybody else who's not the Pristina Corps, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then you see General Perisic goes on and says: "In practice, the commander of the Pristina Corps," Pavkovic, "plans what he has been ordered to, and this is at the request of Sainovic and Minic and the MUP, and so it turns into something like a service of theirs for planning and execution." That sounds like Pavkovic is working for Minic and Sainovic and the MUP in making these plans; wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not fully, Mr. Prosecutor. To me this seems a bit confused. In the previous sentence, he says in cooperation with the civilian part and the MUP to plan and so on and so forth and that Sainovic is to relay that to the MUP. And then he says that he was doing and planning what he had been ordered to upon Sainovic's request and the MUP. On the one hand, we have the MUP and the requests, and on the other hand we have assessments and tasks. To me, the whole text is confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. General, we'll see that the proposal in connection with this problem is: Do not permit the VJ to be commanded outside the system of military subordination and unity of command, right? So that suggests that General Perisic thought there was a problem with the chain of command and subordination, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that is in dispute at all, Mr. Prosecutor. I think I spoke about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 4 talks about bypassing levels of command. General Perisic notes that under the rules of service Milosevic, as supreme commander, can have official conversations with anybody he wants. But he says: "Sometimes you do this without the knowledge of the Chief of Staff," meaning himself, Perisic. Were you aware that that was happening sometimes; and if so, were you aware it happened particularly with General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 5 talks about conducting personnel policies without legal basis, and you'll see it says: "Generals and colonels are frequently promoted, within and without the Supreme Defence Council, without a law or a decree or criteria ..." And at the end of that number 5 he proposes: "No promotion of colonels to generals and of generals to higher rank if this is not in keeping with the law and the proposal by the Chief of Staff." Now, my question is: Two days earlier, on the 21st of July, General Pavkovic was promoted to lieutenant-general, and he told us - we have in an exhibit here, in an interview - he said that was one of two early promotions he got in his career. Based on what you told us before, I take it General Perisic in July 1998 had not made a proposal for General Pavkovic to be promoted, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on. I want to go now back to a couple of collegium sessions, and the next one is 3D644. This is from the 16th of October, 1998. And, General, I need you to look at your page number 11, and in English we're on page 7. It's about five lines down from the top of your page, General, and I think this is you speaking. And, you know, this is about the time of the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement and just before the other agreements were signed later in the month. The last thing you say in that section is: "General, sir, we believe that through the implementation of these activities we do not know what the government will do about the withdrawal of the MUP forces." General Perisic informs you that: "One of the orders has already been" signed. And you said: "I am not sure that they, in their wisdom, will not try and cheat and just move units to other locations ..." Now, why did you say that about the MUP? Did you have some reason to think that they weren't going to comply with the agreements?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, by that time I had had certain experience with all that, and for some reason at that moment I doubted, I had my reasons to suspect that that could happen, especially since it would not have been the first time trying to manipulate the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if in fact they did, in your words, cheat?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I truly couldn't say. I don't know. I know that that evening when there were talks with General Clark and his team, the agreement was for three army units to remain in the area and that the MUP should be downsized to 25 or 28 check-points and that all MUP units in the area of Kosovo which had come from Serbia were to return to their initial locations. As to whether it was done that way at the time, I truly can't say for the very simple reason because I focused, following the Chief of General Staff's task, to work on the work of engagement of security organs and institutions to assist the people of the diplomatic verification mission because a true verification mission and people from it came only about 20 days later, but I was still working on it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the units had to go back to their initial areas, including MUP units, and that was the focus of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your earlier answer: "I had my reasons to suspect that that could happen, especially since it would not have been the first time trying to manipulate the task." Can you tell us about an earlier example of manipulating the task by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, I can't tell you anything specifically, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine if you don't recall a specific incident --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but I knew that some such things had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- otherwise I truly can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me do one more before the break. Exhibit 3D646. This is another VJ collegium. This one's from 26 October 1998. Sir, if you could look at page number 12, and it's page 9 of the English. General, it's the -- I think the second paragraph down from the top of page 12. Again, this is you speaking, and this is the day after, I think, the October agreements with Clark and Naumann had been signed. You say in that second paragraph: "There's another thing that I would like to add to all this, and that is that special attention should now be paid to the chain of command and that units should not be used down there unless they're threatened ..." I take it this is a reference to using VJ units in Kosovo, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I apologise. I wasn't able to follow because on my page 12 there is a part of General Smiljanic's intervention, and then we have Lieutenant-General Obradovic. I am not to be seen on that or the next page; therefore, I wasn't able to follow what you've just read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you look at the bottom of page 11, and I think the last words on that line are your name, and then at the top of the page there are two paragraphs --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that second paragraph, do I need to read it again? You said: "... special attention should now be paid to the chain of command, and units should not be used down there unless they are threatened ..."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read it for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're talking about Kosovo, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is clear because the agreements have been signed, and the internationals are going to be watching closely, and you knew prior to October 1998 there had been instances where units were being used in Kosovo without your knowledge at the General Staff ahead of time, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, that is what had been discussed at various collegium meetings, and the threat of bombing here was truly very big, and I think that we missed it just by a single hair, so to speak, I mean, the fact that we weren't bombed that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you're right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we take our break now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can, Mr. Hannis, but we need to make decisions about timing. We would expect you to be, if possible, less than half an hour. I know that you would wish to be longer, but we're here with limited resources and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I'm trying to focus on material I think will be helpful to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- and that is relevant, and I'm moving as quickly as I can. I'll try to comply with your order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you'll have to comply with it. But in a perfect world, what would you be seeking?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be seeking at least another hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. If we give you half an hour, then if we are able to sit a little later tonight, that would allow us to give two hours to the Defence if they are able to agree on how to divide it up. So with that information in hand, you should address how best you can deal with the situation, and if anything in particular has to be asked of us, THEN you can ask us when we come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: AND we'll resume at 4.15. Mr. Dimitrijevic, we have to have a break at this stage for half an hour. We'll resume at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any further thoughts, Mr. Hannis, on timing now that you've had a chance to think about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll try to do it in 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there somebody who can tell me whether the Defence have been able to agree a disposition of time, or did you try? Did you fail? So will you be able to work out how you would distribute two hours or a little more? I can do two things here. One is to set limits and just get it done, and the other is to ask Mr. Dimitrijevic, who wasn't really told that a third day was a possibility, whether he can accommodate us for, say, an hour or so tomorrow. Now, I was hoping to avoid that, but if that turns out to be necessary, then we will raise it with him in due course, and we will sit for as long as we can today, but that's not going to be significantly beyond 7.00. It might go to half past 7.00. So let's see where we get to, Mr. Hannis. Do your best. If there's something really significant that takes you beyond that time, then tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, we're doing our best to try to finish your evidence in the course of today; as we undertook, we try to do. So if you can, direct your answers as briefly as possible to the particular issues raised. That will help us try and complete the business today. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, next I'd like to look at Exhibit P925. It's a VJ collegium on 27 November. It's page 10 of the English and page 8 in your hard copy, General. You are speaking, and you tell General Ojdanic that there's one incident that you need to speak about, and you say: "When on the night the decision was taken to appoint a new Chief of the General Staff, all barracks, all units, all facilities were placed under full armed control by the MUP and a number of senior officials of the army under the control of state security." Were you one of those senior officers that were placed under control of state security?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. I remember that night very well and that morning too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the evening of the 26th, the previous day, that is, President Milosevic told General Milosevic around 2200 hours that he was being dismissed or replaced. After that I received information from the state security and the MUP --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. You were translated as saying General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter misspoke. General Perisic. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, General, please continue.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we are talking about President Milosevic. President Milosevic called him and told him that he would no longer be the Chief of General Staff. I -- Perisic's idea was to convene his collegium. It could have been around midnight, and I said to him that that should not be done, that we would wait until the morning and that we would discuss things peacefully then. A few days after that, I remember that Mr. Markovic, who was then head of state security, said to me, It's a good thing that you talked Perisic into not having the meeting held at midnight because we would have arrested all of you en route to the General Staff. I had confirmation of that information later on, too, when I talked to other people from the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who would have had the authority to order the MUP to place the army under that kind of control by the police?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's really hard to answer that question, Mr. Prosecutor, the president, through the minister of interior, perhaps directly, as well; I don't know about that. But at any rate, measures had been prepared, and had we gone to this meeting en route we would have been ambushed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me be clear. When you say the president, you mean President Milosevic of the Federal Republic and the minister of the interior for the Republic of Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you could go to page 13 in your version. Now, this was General Ojdanic's first day in the new job, and he says in the second paragraph: "In connection with the first report by General Dimitrijevic, I would not like to make any comments about this at all. This is another proof of many things." There he's referring to what you just said about the army being placed under the control of the MUP when the change was made from Perisic to Ojdanic, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it doesn't have to do with the control over the military over a certain duration of time. We're talking about that night, between the 26th and the 27th of November, 1998. Since President Milosevic had assessed, once he tells General Perisic that he had been replaced, he believed that he could react in an inadequate manner. In the morning, I came to the General Staff, and I first went to see General Ojdanic, congratulated him on his appointment as Chief of General Staff; after that, the collegium meeting was held and the entire hand-over took place peaceably and as required by the rules and regulations. Obviously, someone was afraid of a reaction that did not actually happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me take you to a different meeting now. This is the 10th of December, 1998. It's Exhibit 3D484, and I'm looking at pages 13 through 15 of the English. Yours starts on page 12. Yesterday, Judge Bonomy discussed this partly with you in the part on page 13 where you were talking about the discrepancy between the Pristina Corps and the army, the alienation of the corps commander. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean yesterday's testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember talking with Judge Bonomy about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I recall, your answer was -- you related that to partly these unusual incidents, but I would ask you to go back to page 12 and right above where your name appears and you start speaking, if you would read the last paragraph, which is a paragraph by General Obradovic. And he said: "I'd like to ask you when discussing the overall problem, both in the 3rd Army command and in the corps command there appears some sort of dualism decision-making, some kind of discussion. I would like to ask you that we take clear positions or that we are to know who does what and who's responsible for what and have it defined." You'll see above that he's talking about dealings with the OSCE and how it appears that sometimes the 3rd Army tells them one thing and the Pristina Corps tells them something different. Does that refresh your memory about what the problem was at this time, in December 1998?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, regrettably, I have to say yet again that I don't remember, but now I'm reading this, and this is what my understanding of it is: General Obradovic was speaking about some provocation, or rather, that we as the army had been ambushed in a way because the state was not doing what it was supposed to do. What I'm saying here is that I received this information through different channels and that two teams from the British mission talked with the leadership and the terrorists of the KLA, and they said to them that they had reliable information that the MUP of Serbia was preparing to send some people out in uniforms and to ascribe this to the army. So we had this information, so yet again we were being ambushed. Whatever happened, they could create this provocation which would a priori be ascribed to the army. That is my reaction to that part if that is what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That wasn't actually what I meant --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And thirdly, thirdly -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Up above where you speak, General Obradovic is talking about the 3rd Army commander and the Pristina Corps commander saying different things when dealing with the Federal Commission and the OSCE. Did you see that? Two paragraphs above where your name is.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, let me move on because I have limited time. Despite whatever the particular problem was, would you look at page 14 in the B/C/S, and we're on page 15 of the English. General, near the bottom of page 14 you'll see General Ojdanic speaking, and the second line, it says: "With regard to the conduct of the Pristina Corps, the problem is broader, and allow me and some other people present here to analyse some things and try to resolve it like soldiers and men. It concerns not only the Pristina Corps but also the 3rd Army command. I can't say it before this audience, but yesterday I analysed it thoroughly." Do you know what the problem was with the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army that he's talking about there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Prosecutor, that we have already dealt with part of that yesterday. That is when that group of soldiers who had already completed their term were supposed to go back home and when call-up papers were being issued and when the 3rd Army mobilised more people than had been approved and probably some other things as well. So I don't know what the general said -- well, but yesterday -- I don't know what he is saying here. He said: "Yesterday I viewed this exactly." That is what he says, and he says that he's trying to deal with it in a soldierly and human way. I assume that he talked to the corps commander and President Milosevic; that is my assumption. That's the only way in which he could have meant this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me take you to another collegium session. This is Exhibit P928, a meeting on the 30th of December, 1998. You talked about part of this before, yesterday, with Judge Bonomy. I need you to look at page 14 in your B/C/S, and it's also page 14 in the English. You see your name there, General, and I want to go to the second paragraph from the bottom. And you mention that -- you mention General Marjanovic. And right after that, you say: "I think that it is a priority to ensure that not even Sainovic or any other Sainovic can solve these problems by lightly deciding to use the units." Does that not mean that prior to this date Mr. Sainovic had somehow been engaged in decisions to use the VJ units?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, no. The context in which I said this was not to allow that to happen; namely, that everything should be done, that no civilians, no one outside the chain of command, no one outside the military can use the units of the army. This was a general position, and I insisted upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know -- let me stop you --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since from time to time --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Why did you use Mr. Sainovic's name in that context? That's consistent with what you told Donnelly and Crosland, isn't it, that he was involved in how the VJ units were being used, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Fila on his feet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I never said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we will be wasting a lot of time if people speak inaccurately. Mr. Dimitrijevic never said that he had said that to Donnelly. You asked him twice, and both times he said that he had never said that to Donnelly and this other man, Crosland, whatever his name was. And if you put that kind of question, we will stay here for three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I doubt if we'll be here for three days, Mr. Fila. It's for us to decide whether to believe Mr. Dimitrijevic's version or the Crosland version of the -- of what was said. So Mr. Hannis puts it on one basis, but we're capable, perfectly capable, of assessing both versions when we come to look at all the evidence at the end of the case. Mr. Hannis, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're saying you never said that Sainovic was using the VJ units; is that your claim?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Sainovic was using VJ units? That is something I've never said to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But he was, wasn't he, whether you said it or not. You know he was, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Prosecutor, I said what I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, you said -- no, stop, stop --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- however, I never said that he had used the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You saw General Perisic's letter, Exhibit P717, where he complained about how the army was being commanded outside the chain of command and complained, in particular naming Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Minic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Again, there is an inaccurate representation of the document. Show the witness the document, and you will see that the word used is "attempt." Attempt is the word that's used twice. What was attempted was not done because if something is attempted and then done, then it is done. It is no longer an attempt. That's the way it is in Anglo-Saxon law, in the English language, in our language, any language. So if you want to get something from the witness that is not good, try to do it fairly and honestly. Read what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think looking at my question there's nothing inconsistent with the document the way I framed the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me, but Mr. Fila's complaint is that all it says is that there's an attempt to command the army outside the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here's the letter. It's right on your screen, paragraph 3: "Attempt to command ..." Attempt, I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. My problem here is that I need three screens today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the question should be formulated in accordance with paragraph 3 of that letter, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of my time I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll make allowances for this sort of difficulty arising, and you shouldn't be discouraged -- we're not going to have a record that reflects that somehow or other you were railroaded into a position that you say later is unsatisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, that's all right, Your Honour. I think given the witness's attitude about this, I'm going to move on to something that may be more constructive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Exhibit P939, General, is a VJ collegium dated the 21st of January, 1999. Now, I think you told us previously that you didn't know about the Joint Command by that name in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999; is that correct? Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I said was that I heard that different names were being used: Joint Command, coordination staff, and multi-disciplinary staff, and so on and so forth. I don't know what it is here, but please, if I said something could you read that out to me, what it was that I had said, because I really cannot keep in my head every sentence I uttered over five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I just want to make the point that you yourself used the point "Joint Command" in January 1999. It's at page 24 in your B/C/S; it's page 26 of the English. This is a day you all were having a discussion and in part about Racak, and at the bottom of page 26 in the English, it's near the middle of the page.
