You make a reference to General Marjanovic's dilemma, and then you say: "I don't know what is being presented there and whether what is being presented by the Joint Command is this or something else entirely ..." So you referred to that body down in Kosovo as the Joint Command at least on one occasion, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I think that it would only be fair if you read the next sentence to me, as well, where it says, I quote --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you just answer my question. You used the term to refer to that body down in Kosovo as the Joint Command, right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is impossible to interpret when there are two speakers speaking at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, perhaps somebody did -- I did use it, but I meant coordination, MUP and the military, because -- allow me to say this. In this sentence, it says I was personally present when the minister of the interior was received here by the Chief of General Staff and when the man unequivocally said that the backbone of terrorism had been broken, the terrorism had been destroyed, and this was a showdown with the remnants or remains of gangs and terrorists. I think that it is perfectly obvious who and what I meant and that you can draw a conclusion about that. For me, it was the MUP and the military, but probably somebody in their previous statements mentioned something, this Joint Command. So then I mentioned it, too, in that sense, but unequivocally I meant the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And earlier in that same meeting, General Ojdanic used the term to refer to that body down there as the Joint Command, right? Do you remember that? You saw that page yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not remember that he called it that because, indeed, December 1998 was a long time ago. Possibly he used the term, and I relied on that. So what was in my mind was the MUP, the army, coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me take you to February 4th, Exhibit P932 -- or, I'm sorry, I don't want to do that one. Let me move to February 25th, Exhibit P941, at page 14 and 15. You're talking about Pavkovic having brought in a part of the 72nd Special Brigade into Kosovo without you having received any prior notification about that. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe it's page 14 and 15, at the bottom of 14 going on to page 15.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 14. Yes, I found it. 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's correct that General Pavkovic had during the time that the October agreements were pending brought in this additional element into Kosovo in violation of that agreement and without informing you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, first of all Pavkovic could not have ordered the anti-terrorist battalion of the 72nd Special Brigade to move towards, not to but towards Kosovo and Metohija because such an order could only be issued by the Chief of the General Staff. And since yesterday we talked about this, and I remember that I reacted then to say why this unit was being sent down there; it was not sent to Kosovo. On the orders of the Chief of the General Staff, it was sent to the rim of Kosovo. That was at the time when terrorism was already escalating. That was why it was sent to the rim of Kosovo in accordance with the orders that we discussed yesterday and today about how units can be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I complained because I wasn't aware of this unit being moved because I, as the chief of the security administration, was in charge, or rather, I was the mainstay in professional terms of this. The commanders decided on the use of the units, but we in the service were those who made sure that the units are not misused but are used properly for specific tasks. And this unit should always have been used in its entirety, not to be broken up into elements. That is why I sent a team from the security administration to check how the unit was being used, why it was being used, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But in fact --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as far as I can recall, it was sent to the rim.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But in fact, it also moved into the interior, did it not? You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is why I sent this team down there to check what was happening when I learned that the unit had gone there. That was precisely because I was mistrustful, so to speak, because I was afraid that instead of remaining at the rim of Kosovo it would go further in, and that's exactly what happened, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At whose order did it go in?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you now at this point, but probably it was the 3rd Army that decided that because it was also moved closer -- this unit was moved closer to the rim of Kosovo at the request of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, General, I don't mean to be rude, but I do need to move along. I want to show you next Exhibit P938, 938. This is another VJ collegium from the 18th of March. You already spoke yesterday about a part of this. Two things I want to ask you about: One is at page 21 of the English, page 18 and 19 for you. You told us yesterday about the problems with attacks being reported in what you suspected sometimes VJ had initiated action. But your second question, and it's at the bottom of page 18, regarded unusual incidents. And you talk about an incident in Leskovac, apparently, where there were some 200 drunken conscripts involved in what you refer to as shenanigans. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was this a part of an ongoing problem you had with the 3rd Army in failing to report --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you would then go to page 25 -- or 22 of the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it is possible that this was contained in the report from the 3rd Army. I can't say that, but when I spoke about extraordinary incidents yesterday, well, this is one such instance, when conscripts --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- are not under control and then they engage in this kind of shenanigans, if I may call it that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have to move along. Page 22 and 23 in your B/C/S, General Ojdanic is speaking. I think it's the second big paragraph on that page, page 25 of the English. He mentions that: "All the major decisions regarding the use of the army in accordance with the authorisation from the competent body, the president of the FRY ..." But then he goes on and says: "It's obvious that something here is not right, and I will call and talk to the 3rd Army commander about that, and I also think that should be followed by him coming here so that we can sit down and talk properly on the subject" -- "on this subject ..." Do you know after this meeting on the 18th of March, did General Ojdanic actually call General Pavkovic and/or have him come in to talk about the problems?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that for sure, but I assume that General Ojdanic did call him. I assume that for a very simple reason, because in those days this problem kept cropping up with increasing frequency at the collegium meetings. That was just a couple of days before I left, let me remind you, so that at that time I already did not receive quite a lot of information. I assume that this was the case because whenever he said at the collegium meetings that something should be done, then it was -- it got translated into tasks. So I assume that this was the case now, but obviously there was a problem vis-a-vis the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You have no personal knowledge whether that actually happened, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, about five, seven more minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you mentioned meetings you went to in -- I think you recall July and August 1998, meetings with Mr. Milosevic, General Perisic, the highest-ranking people in the army, in the VJ. I would ask you, General Pavkovic has provided information to us in interviews. He mentions five such meetings, and he dated the first one as the 31st of May, 1998. This is from pages 321 through 329 and at page 395 of his interview, which is Exhibit P949. He mentions you as being a person in attendance at those meetings, and the other meetings in addition to 31 May he said took place on 21 July, 4 August 1998, 31 August 1998, and a fifth meeting in January 1999, where instead of General Perisic, General Ojdanic attended. General Pavkovic was the 3rd Army commander instead of General Samardzic, and he mentions Mr. Milutinovic and Mr. Sainovic as attending those meetings. Would you disagree with him about either the dates or the persons attending those meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I said that I unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters couldn't hear the rest of the answer because of technical difficulties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, whether those were the exact dates, I can't tell you, but there were three, four, five, six such meetings. I think that I attended all of the meetings in 1998, but that meeting that you mention in January 1999, not only did I not attend this meeting, but until this moment I was unaware of this meeting ever being held. But it just proves the point that I have already made: At that time, I was already sidelined.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think your part of the answer about who attended the meeting and whether Mr. Milutinovic and Mr. Sainovic were at those meetings was lost due to a technical difficulty. Can you repeat whether you would dispute General Pavkovic's statement regarding those two being at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I said that I attended the meetings in 1998, but as for the meeting in January 1999, this is the first that I hear of it. As regards the presence of those persons, I think that at all the meetings that were held in 1998 Mr. Sainovic was one of the participants. Now, as for Mr. Milutinovic, the then-president of Serbia, I cannot be that certain. There were several meetings that I attended and that he attended too. It is quite possible that he did attend one of those meetings, but I cannot claim that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Two last items, one relates to Joint Command. Yesterday at page 21, you said: "It's my impression that at a later stage it was supposed to serve somebody's purposes, and by that I mean General Pavkovic, to cover some of his activities so that he could say, I have the Joint Command behind me." Cover what activities? What were you referring to when you said that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably the use of some units or elements of units of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this expression, staff command and so on, that something was being decided there, this is where it came from, Pristina. And yesterday I said that I had never seen any such paper. I know how a command is established, and if you allow me half a minute I think it might be of some use to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in 1998 alone --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- maybe one of the other lawyers will ask you --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to say about the controls or checks that were carried out by the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please, I have to move on. From whom would Pavkovic need cover? To whom would he be saying, I have the Joint Command behind me.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably when a question was asked down the chain of command why a unit was used or why an element of a unit was used by the army commander, the Chief of General Staff, well, probably it was easier to say, Somebody told me that, or any other kind of excuse along those lines, but not to specify who said that. And that is probably the result of that. I am now speculating as to the possible reason because I really can't deal with this question in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The last thing, General - I thank you for your time - I want to ask you relates to what you told Judge Bonomy today about the circumstances when you were told by Mr. Milosevic that you were being removed from your position and you declined what he offered for you to do instead. And you explained that one of the reasons behind your removal was because certain people didn't like the way you were speaking up about what they were doing. And isn't that consistent -- weren't you just the third or fourth one in a line of people who weren't doing things the way Mr. Milosevic and General Pavkovic wanted them, and specifically I mean General Samardzic, General Perisic, and Jovica Stanisic all had been removed from their positions before you got removed, and they had all been complaining about General Pavkovic and General Milosevic and how things were being done with regard to the army under those two, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you could put it that way, but I think, Mr. Prosecutor, that what we're dealing here first of all is a shift in the policy and that people who opposed certain things were simply not acceptable anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. I don't have any more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe we don't have any questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, first of all, good day, Mr. Dimitrijevic, please bear with us for a moment. First, I would like to ask you to complete the thought that you started when the Prosecution interrupted you. What was it that you wanted to say about the checks by the General Staff? You told us that we would learn something, and then you were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I thought that this might be important when we were talking about the issues that I was questioned about. When we're talking about this -- since stress is being placed on this Joint Command, probably rightly so because this term is contained in some papers. I can say that -- based on my recollection, I can say that I think that in 1998 there were four or five inspections carried out led personally by the Chief of the General Staff. The last one was in December, and I think it was led by the then-Chief of Staff, General Ojdanic; all the others were led by General Perisic. It is inconceivable for me to imagine that the Chief of the General Staff would come to Pristina with his team, 30 or 40 strong, and not to be received by highest-ranking command in the garrison. So he would always come to the Pristina Corps command, and nobody ever told him there based on the papers that I saw because after every inspection there would be reports and the President Milosevic was also made aware of those reports and the tasks that the corps, the army, should carry out and the tasks that are in the purview of the General Staff; so it is quite inconceivable for me to understand how somebody could go there five times and not notice this Joint Command and not sit down with the Joint Command and discuss those issues. Quite simply, nobody mentioned the existence of any other command outside of the Pristina Corps command. There was mention of coordination and cooperation with the MUP, but as far as the commands are concerned not a single letter was written about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that no Joint Command was ever in command of the Pristina Corps based on your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my knowledge, no command except for the corps commander. And in my interventions at the collegium meetings, I insisted that everything must be done to prevent, since names of people who were down there were being bandied about, that -- prevent that any of them would make decisions or use the troops, which would be very bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So can we agree, then, that nothing of the sort ever happened, that no Sainovics, no Minics, or no other civilians ever commanded the 3rd Army, the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean that nothing of the sort happened? But I do agree with you that civilians did not exercise command. It was the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So the chain of command in the Army of Yugoslavia was intact in that sense?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, in the essence it was the case. The only problem was that the reports that were coming in were not always realistic. They did not depict the real situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, fair enough. Let us complete this topic. You as the chief of the security administration on any basis, whether through reports that you got from your security officers or through private channels or any other channels or in any other way, for instance, as you had coffee with somebody, did you ever learn that Nikola Sainovic exercised command over the Army of Yugoslavia, that he had any command role over Ojdanic, that he had effective control over the whole of Army of Yugoslavia, including yourself, because all of those issues, all of those claims were made here without any corroboration, but this is what we have on record here.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that you made me laugh.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I sent my own inspections to Kosovo, to the Pristina Corps area. Reports were written. All the reports, again, were sent to the president. The security administration gathered lots of information and sent it to the president, and this was not written in any single report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Least of all that Sainovic would come to the General Staff and issue orders to Perisic, Ojdanic, myself, well, this really made me laugh.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, it would have made me laugh, too, if I weren't in a situation to be defending a man who is in Detention Unit. All kinds of claims are being made here. I want to ask you something else. You said yesterday that in wartime a part of the General Staff with the chief was in communication with the supreme commander, which was -- and who was President Milosevic. Was it necessary to have somebody between the Chief of the General Staff and Milosevic to relay orders?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think so -- well, they were not in the same premises, but they were -- or rather, not in the same room, but they were in the same building.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please slow down and make pauses between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, interpreters, I don't have much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said yesterday that General Pavkovic was in direct communication with President Milosevic. You said that he spent two weeks there and so on. What does it mean, direct communication? Could you please clarify that a little bit? Did he have access to him and -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try. He had communication with him because President Milosevic would call him on the phone. I don't know what they talked about, but it was one of the questions that I asked of President Milosevic when we realized that our phones in the Pristina Corps command were being wire-tapped. That is why I asked him, If this is not done on your orders then you will not fare well yourself. So he did have communication, line of communication. It could have been over the phone. He would go to Belgrade and not report to anyone, to the Chief of General Staff; that's what I mean. The army commander was not aware of that. I know that later on they would visit each other in private capacity, birthdays, family visits, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that, but did he need Sainovic then to establish communication with Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I think that on the basis of everything that I said that would directly follow that -- it would directly follow that he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, to complete this story, that being as it is, is there any possibility for you when you received him - so I'm talking about foreign diplomats, the British ambassador, whoever - for you to tell them that Sainovic was the one through whom Sainovic is relaying orders, receiving orders, that he was his operational -- that there was this operational diary or whatever. Is there a theoretical possibility that you did express this kind of a thought?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Speakers are kindly asked to speak one at a time. It is impossible to interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dimitrijevic, the interpreters are having some difficulty because you're speaking immediately after Mr. Fila completes his question. To allow the interpreters to catch up into whatever language they're translating the evidence, could you please just pause for a little time before answering each question. Now, as a result the last answer was not interpreted, so could you answer that question again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, could we have the question repeated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The same thing happened again. Two speakers are speaking at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my answer was that I did not say anything like that to anyone because if I had said that I would have worked against myself because I always raised this issue of subordination and command at every collegium meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Fine. Let us move on to a different topic. Mr. Dimitrijevic, a couple of weeks ago, we had General Milan Djakovic testify here as a Court witness. In 1998, he was a colonel or a lieutenant-colonel, and he was the operations officer of General Pavkovic. Do you know this man?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I met him sometime after the air-strikes at a reception for -- to commemorate the army day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In his testimony, in particular when the Trial Chamber asked questions, he insisted that the term the "Joint Command" was invented by him together with Pavkovic and that when those civilians appeared in Kosovo in the period between July and October, as he said, and I see that you said the same thing, that Pavkovic said that those meetings should continue to be called the Joint Command. In other words, he confirmed that the author of the term "Joint Command" was Nebojsa Pavkovic. My question to you is this: Do you believe -- do you tend to believe that rather than the memo that was read to you by Judge Bonomy - we don't know who the source of this information was - to the effect that Slobodan Milosevic invented this term "Joint Command"? Which is the most -- more probable option?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question is whether it was invented by President Milosevic or by Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think, Mr. Fila, that President Milosevic did not need to invent anything; he was the president at that time. So the answer is that this was needed as cover for General Pavkovic. He needed this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is pure speculation, Mr. Fila. Let's move to something concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If General Djakovic, the operations officer of General Pavkovic, keeps notes or minutes at those meetings, do you think that he is in a position to know what the name of the meeting is? And he said that he termed those meetings "Joint Command" in agreement with Pavkovic. What do you think? Does he know what he's talking about?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can see counsel being reluctant to intervene in a situation where the witness is being brought here by us, but again, that's a matter for the Trial Chamber and is not for this witness to analyse.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yesterday, you talked about Lieutenant-Colonel Momir Stojanovic having informed you of certain meetings which he did not attend. I won't go into any further detail because of the time.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that in your opinion it was a type of cooperation between the MUP and army. In that cooperation, did any civilians participate in it or, according to your information, was it only done by the army and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the reports I received from the Pristina Corps and the security organ as well as in personal contact over the phone with lieutenant-colonel Stojanovic, he told me that he does not take part at those meetings, that he is not in attendance, and that with General Pavkovic there is always General Djakovic accompanying him, I believe, and that there are MUP representatives there who are in attendance as well as some civilians referred to here. When I asked him what was going on, he said, Well, there was nothing for us there, I do not attend those meetings, and as a service we did not deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be the last stage of my questioning. I want to ask you about the famous letter of -- by Perisic. It is Exhibit P717. Let us not be hasty concerning this letter because it seems you were rushed through it by the Prosecutor, and I will take it slowly. Look at item 3 at page 162, I believe --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Item 3: "An attempt to control the Army of Yugoslavia by unauthorised persons ..." What does it mean, attempt?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, an attempt is when you are attempting to do something but you fail. An attempt means that you have an idea about trying to do something but you fail to -- well, in any case attempts can be successful and unsuccessful.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In sub-item (a), what does Perisic say? Who is trying to command the army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To subordinate units -- well, the MUP. The general is talking about the MUP. He's talking about this constant wish on the part of the MUP to have some of our units subordinated to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So MUP, not Nikola Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, one of the things we've tried to avoid with the witness is going over things that speak for themselves. This is a matter that you can make submissions to us about. Why is it you need to address it directly with the witness? When it was addressed by Mr. Hannis, it was because the witness had seen the letter, was able to tell us a bit about Perisic's position; he saw it at an important stage after it had been sent, for example, and these things were all established by evidence. But we don't want an analysis done by this witness of that letter. If there's something he can personally tell us that will be of significance, please turn to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We heard Momir Bulatovic here, page 13921 and you let him read the letter, as well, and then he told you something about the meaning of the word "attempt" in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Defence counsel, I never provided that letter --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When we go to sub-item (b), after having read that, my question for you is this: Rather than interpreting what Perisic wanted to say, because you've already been asked by the Chamber about that and you said it was some sort of confusion, but do you have some personal knowledge as the head of administration that what actually is stated here took place, that Sainovic tried or, indeed, controlled the VJ? Please read the sub-item (b). Have you ever come across any information that would corroborate what is stated here or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Defence counsel, the sub-item begins with the word "attempt." There is no mention of anything being completed successfully. There was an attempt to have this or that happen -- rather, to have Sainovic and Minic --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask you. Did you have some such information?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic -- Mr. Dimitrijevic, the next counsel to examine you will be Mr. Visnjic, who represents General Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, before beginning I'd first like to ask for clarification from you. Perhaps there's something you can confirm for me, and it is in the documents, but I want to have it corrected in the transcript. Today, in one of your answers you said that there were several inspections carried out by the General Staff which visited the command of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps and that they were headed by the chiefs of the General Staff and that one of them was headed by General Ojdanic. You said that that inspection was in December 1998. Since there is documentation in existence, would you allow for a possibility that it was in early March 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible for the simple reason that Ojdanic became the Chief of the General Staff, and I know that at one of the collegium meetings said that he was to head the team personally and that he wanted to acquaint himself with the situation personally. Therefore, it could have been in January or February rather than in December, but that's why I said that he headed one inspection in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look at Exhibit 939, which is collegium meetings, P939, collegium meetings of the 21st of January. Mr. Haider is going to help us. It's in the Chamber's binder. I'm interested in page 28, paragraph 4 in the English, and page 31, paragraph 3 in English. In B/C/S, it is page 28, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: While Mr. Riaz is looking for it, I want to remind you this is the minutes which you referred to the Racak events and the participation of the army. A working group was established, so that was supposed to deal with -- it is K05222069 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: P939, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the meeting, a working group was established which, among other things, dealt with the problem of reporting. I would kindly ask you to read the paragraph. General, my question has to do with how in your view General Ojdanic requested from his subordinates to tackle this issue. Did he encourage them within their respective authorities to investigate and carry out checks?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he did. Every time a question was tabled concerning which we were unsure of whether reports were good or not, he usually insisted that we use all possible lines to inquire. This part whereby he mentions the principles of subordination, as stated and written here, he allowed for a possibility that some of the subordinates contacted president directly --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, the paragraph below.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This group -- yes, let me read it first. Yes, I've nothing to add. This is completely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, at the collegium meetings we kept receiving reports, which spoke of the failure to act --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, you've already testified about that.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Another thing which has to do with reporting as well. If you recall, it has to do with the events mentioned at the collegium meeting of the 10th of December concerning problems with extraordinary events. You've explained to the Chamber what those were. Do you remember General Ojdanic ordering that he should personally be informed on any extraordinary incident or event?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he did because he said that such incidents and events have to be examined carefully and that all levels responsible need to undertake measures. When such incidents occurred, usually it will be dealt with by the General Staff rather than at the level where it took place; therefore, there were comments for the army command to be made as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to mention for the Chamber that this is 3D559; in the English, page 20, paragraphs 2 and 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: To go back to an exhibit which was shown on a number of occasions today, it is P938. It is collegium meetings of the 18th of March, 1998. Judge Bonomy asked you about the portion of it where rampage is mentioned without knowledge of the corps command. The Prosecutor asked you something, as well, about the same paragraph. You explained to him -- it is paragraph 25 in English. You explained to him that General Ojdanic requested and probably talked to the 3rd Army commander.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, it is Exhibit P938. In the English, it is page 25; in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could Mr. Riaz show you 3D682. While we're waiting for it, I wanted to ask you this: The General Staff's concern had to do with the situation at the time trying not to provoke a NATO intervention, not to give them any reason to. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: A number of your complaints had to do with that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The talks in Rambouillet were getting to their end. We knew how things went. There were threats issued by the West on a daily basis, and it was our assessment that it literally depended on at what hour the bombing would begin rather than the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This document was issued by the General Staff two days following the collegium meeting.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Have a look at it and tell me -- first of all, concerning the comments of rampage, so-called rampage, mentioned at the collegium meetings. Does this correspond to the comments made?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, yes. This describes the situation and its complexity in more detail. When it comes to the Siptar, or rather, terrorist forces and the foreign elements as well as dangers which were clearly visible and, of course, when reference is made to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've had that suggestion -- I mean, it -- unless there's some problem in translation, it's very difficult to see that this is a reference to KLA activity or terrorist activity. It -- reading it in English, it looks clearly to be a reference to actions of forces of the state without the knowledge of their superiors. And in any event, if we're talking about an argument over interpretation, that's not for this witness; that's something we can deal with in another situation. But it's very difficult to read it the way you're suggesting, that these are rampages against the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I see this as a preventive document which was to prevent any sort of action. That's why it's called warning. It was supposed to warn the subordinate commands that any such activities should be curtailed, having in mind the consequences those could bring about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The minute clearly says action has to be taken against these outrageous attacks. No one would dispute that. You're pushing an open door on that here. The question is how you react, and that seems to be what the rampage is referring to, overreaction. But you can address that in your submissions to us in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we are still on the same collegium meeting. I would like to ask you to have a look at 3D1073 [as interpreted]. When answering some of the Prosecutor's questions, you mentioned the way the collegium worked, and you talked about the tasks which were issued. As far as you can recall, this document representing the tasks from the collegium meetings, can it be included in the measures undertaken by the General Staff as regards the issue of reporting and reports which were sent from the lower to higher commands, especially having in mind item 1?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, counsel. This is it. When I talked about the work the -- the way the collegium worked, I said that at the close of each meeting the Chief of the General Staff addressed the meeting and then issued tasks. This was done so that there would be a conclusion rather than all of us having sit around the table and then leave without having done anything. Each of the meetings was attended by chef de cabinet of the General Staff. In this case, it was Mr. Vlajkovic, and it was presented to all of the participants so that they could all implement their respective tasks within the dead-lines set.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let me ask you another thing. Over these two days, you testified about Podujevo and what the Chief of General Staff did and about Racak and what the Chief of General Staff did. And today, we looked at these comments that had to do with the work group and the encouragement of subordinates to analyse reports. We also looked at evidence related to the collegium meetings held on the 4th and 18th of March. In relation to the period during which you worked with General Ojdanic, can you tell me whether General Ojdanic was sincere in his efforts to truly find out what it was that was going on, or rather, what the problems were in reporting; or, quite simply, did he turn the other way? What is your view on this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No doubt, yes, he was sincere in these efforts. As for the extent to which he succeeded, I cannot speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm saying yes, he wanted to, but the question is whether he managed every time to bring things to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether it would be the right time to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be helpful if you continued for a little while, Mr. Visnjic. We'll probably have a 20-minute break, and then we're going to try to go to half past 7.00. So we need to have no more than about an hour and a half. If you can get to quarter to 6.00, that would be ideal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the records of the collegium meetings that you read yesterday and today, do they correspond to your own recollection of the discussions at the collegium? I'm referring particularly to 1998 -- the end of 1998 and the beginning of 1999.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are some details that I remember with full accuracy. They're really striking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the collegium ever look the any plan that considered the option of expelling the Albanian population from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any such plan or did I ever attend any such deliberations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I assume that, then, your answer would be no to my following question, whether this thesis was mentioned as a solution in terms of the control of Serbia over the territory at the meetings that you attended, at least?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that in 1998 most of the high officers in the General Staff were against the extensive use of the military in the fight against terrorism. My question is: To the best of your recollection - and we have quite a few records of the collegium, so we don't really have to go into all of that - can you remember what General Ojdanic's position was with regard to that matter?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that he talked about that before he was Chief of General Staff and when he became chief and that that was precisely why he insisted that the chain of command had to function and that the army should be in the function prescribed by the constitution and by laws. So I don't think that he differed on that score, either. The -- namely, that the worst way of using the military was exactly the way in which it was being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. That was not, with respect, an answer to the question, Mr. Dimitrijevic. The question was whether General Ojdanic was against the extensive use of the military in the fight against terrorism, and all you told us was that he believed in obeying the chain of command. Now, can you answer the question that you were asked. Was he against, as you were, the extensive use of the military in the fight against terrorism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he was, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what did he do about it once he was Chief of the General Staff to sort out the fact that the army was being used outwith the border area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really cannot tell you. I know what he said at the collegium meetings and what I said. As for what he did in direct communication with the president, I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even more so because my position by then was a bit worse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is what I'm going to ask you, General. In your view, did the Army of Yugoslavia observe the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the General Staff, yes; but as for the army as the army, that is to say some parts, I don't think it did. But basically, if you are referring to the withdrawal of units, if you mean the withdrawal of units into the garrisons, yes, that was honoured.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us look at a document, please. It is the 21st of January, General Obradovic's remarks -- or rather, let's try to do it without the document. At that meeting, General Obradovic claims that the army is observing the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement but that at the same time the situation had changed from October onwards, bearing in mind that the KLA grew into a respectable force at that point -- I'm sorry. It is the collegium of the 2nd of February, 1999, page 9 in B/C/S. So bearing in mind that then it numbered some 12 to 15.000 men, am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And these are the objections that we raised all the time, namely, that at one point the verification mission is going to verify what the situation was, and by then everything will have been too late. That is to say after the agreement the military honoured their obligations, they withdrew into garrisons, and as for these empty areas the KLA entered straight away, and the situation thereby became more complicated and escalated. We said that to General Clark that night, too, that that would happen; however, of course, the agreement had been signed, and as far as that is concerned, we had fully carried it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, at the time, at collegium meetings didn't you make a certain assertion that there would be a problem in relation to the agreement because the side that controls the crisis on the one hand is concentrating on restricting the security forces of the Army of Yugoslavia, and on the other hand they are giving the KLA free reign, and in this way they can provoke the security forces?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, counsellor. That's what I said on a few occasions because whenever we raised the issue at a few meetings with President Milosevic, what we were told is we did not accept a foreign presence, a foreign force; we accepted civilians. My knowledge from that period is as follows, I remember some of the details even today, that 90 per cent of the verification mission were active-duty officers of the armies that took part in the setting up of the mission except that they were not in uniform, and they all came from intelligence structures, from the intelligence community. That is to say that we had quite a few cases when we realized that members of the verification mission were actually transferring weapons and providing information about the Army of Yugoslavia. So really, they sided with the Albanian terrorists. At the same time, they asked and in many cases they actually overstepped, they went beyond their mandate, and they asked for information that they were not authorised to ask about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the time for the break has come now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, there are limits to which repetitive evidence is appropriate in the context of this witness. It's plain from the minutes that he repeatedly complained that it was unfair that the KLA were in a position to occupy the vacuum, and he's amplified the answer to some extent along lines that we've heard a number of witnesses deal with already. Please try to concentrate on things that either have to be challenged because of what he's said already or that are peculiarly matters within his knowledge that he can assist us with. Mr. Dimitrijevic, we will have another break now. It will be a bit shorter this time. We'll resume at ten minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, could you please look at 3D685. This is an assessment of the intelligence and security situation and danger to the security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. My question is, first of all, General: Can you confirm that you took part in the writing of this document and that you signed it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsellor, I don't believe that I signed it. I could only sign the attachment about security that was taken from the security administration to the General Staff when this assessment was being compiled whenever these assessments were made. As for the paper of the security administration is concerned, my deputy usually went to the General Staff with that, and over the last few years it had been Colonel Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I assume that Colonel Gajic went there with the agreed views of the security administration?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. He went with a final paper so that what we concluded could be incorporated in this assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you look at the last page of this document where the conclusions are. E-court, it is page 3D0501 --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, I see it. I see that all the chiefs signed this, so my signature is there, and that is quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question, General. Bearing in mind what happened after this assessment, can you tell us to what extent this assessment was justified, and could you perhaps tell us whether you agree with the conclusions that were presented at the end of this assessment?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is to say it was realistic, it was justified, because the Chief of General Staff had requested this assessment precisely so that, I assume, he could present this assessment to the top echelons of the state, and I believe that it was submitted to the members of the Supreme Defence Council since we're talking about February 1999; and these conclusions are basically correct. As for the foreign factor, it came from the assessments of the intelligence administration, so absolutely, all of us as -- as long as we signed it, of course, we were in agreement, especially in view of avoiding any conflict with NATO as stated in paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That's exactly what I wanted to ask you about. Thank you, General. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Dimitrijevic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Aleksic on behalf of General Pavkovic. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, yesterday on page 81 of the transcript you said -- since you had been asked about reporting, you said that every morning you read the combat report of the Pristina Corps. My question in relation to this is whether during the summer of 1998 and throughout 1998 you read, or rather, received combat reports that were sent by the command of the 3rd Army from the forward command post in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, counsellor. As a matter of fact, what you said at first -- well, the combat reports from the Pristina Corps did not come to the General Staff throughout the year. It was only later, sometime towards the end of the year, that they started coming in because that was what was requested in -- irrespective of the army report that the corps report be sent in. Yes, every morning. I read everything that had arrived during the course of the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So, General, you don't know what General Samardzic reported to General Perisic if you had not seen these reports; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see these reports. They went along the chain of command, and they were sent to the office of the Chief of General Staff because that is the chain of command, and I was not the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: All right. General, although you have not seen this, please look at one of these reports at least. Could Riaz Haider please show you 4D142. General, do you know that the 3rd Army in the summer of 1998 had its forward command post in Pristina and that General Samardzic --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know. I know that in accordance with the order of the commander of the 3rd Army the forward command post was activated, and if I remember correctly I believe that at first the chief of the army staff was there, General Simic, and then the commander of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: All right. General, you have the document in front of you, so could you please look at page 2 now. In English, it's also page 2, paragraph 3, and it says: "Situation in the army units." Have you had a look?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Am I right, General, this report was signed by General Mladenovic and the combat groups are reported here and the axes and the activities that are being carried out in the area in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you please have a look at the next page, page 3, paragraph 5, that is. On behalf of General Samardzic, General Mladenovic says that General Samardzic decided as follows inter alia: "Continue the blockade of the villages of Junik, Jasic, and support MUP forces in breaking up terrorist forces in the areas of the village of Baboloc, Prilep, and Glodjane."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what's written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, the date of this document is the 10th of August, right? That can be seen on the first page.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, let's be very specific about this: 1998. Isn't that right, General, the 10th of August, 1998?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I've said yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, earlier on you talked about these inspections and tours of units by the General Staff, and you will agree with me that in the period from the 10th until the 13th of August, 1998, a big team headed by the Chief of General Staff, General Perisic, toured the units in Kosovo and Metohija; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allow for the possibility that that is the correct date. There were a few during the course of the year, as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Fine. General, could you now please look at 4D526.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So, General, am I right if I say that General Obradovic, Milorad Obradovic, as part of the General Staff team is reporting from the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica to the Chief of General Staff on the 13th of August, 1998, about this tour?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's sending this to the General Staff but not to the Chief of the General Staff, although it is addressed to the chief because the chief was actually leading this inspection team.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Okay. So, General, this is the third paragraph that I want you to look at where it says -- well, in the second paragraph it says that the commander of the 3rd Army briefed the team and then the commander of the Pristina Corps and the commander of the special units, that was General Stanimirovic, about the -- that they briefed the chief about the combat-readiness in the units and the tasks that were carried out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, it says "The briefing of the commander of the 3rd Army, the Pristina Corps, and the special units corps in terms of contents and questions were at the appropriate level and served the function of the objectives and the tasks of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, we don't really need this witness to read things from documents to us. We can read these, and you can submit -- make submissions about them. That's not advancing the case any. So please try to confine your questions to things of which he has personal knowledge or things that you require to challenge as a result of what he said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, this pertains to his previous testimony. Let me ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you know of any specific example, any specific actions, where General Pavkovic carried out without the approval of General Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you want me to be specific now, I really can't do that after ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I know that such things happened on the basis of the reports of the army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you, General. Could you now please look -- since you said that in the reports -- that you did not have any reports about the locations of the units or actions they were engaged in. Could you please look at 4D131. 4D131. I have this document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm advised this document is not released in e-court. Is this a document that's not already exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I have a hard copy here, and according to my information it was in e-court. But the reason why I'm showing it to the witness is because it was not admitted into evidence during the trial so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's not in e-court either, so you need to move to something else, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, am I right when I say that sometime in August 1998 in the General Staff that operational duty teams were set up that monitored the situation in the units in the field in Kosovo, that practically every collegium meeting started by the head of the operations team submitting a detailed report to the collegium about the location of the units, the situation at the border, the situation in the area, the actions that were taken, where MUP was given support, and that somebody from those officers, either General Paja Smiljanic or General Terzic or some of the colonels from the first administration showed the location of the forces of the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army on slides or on maps when the need arose.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsellor, the operations team always existed as part of the duty service of the General Staff. The size depended on the situation. I assume that you're talking about the team that was established in the second half, at a later stage, in light of the fact that the situation in Kosovo and Metohija got more complicated. Yes, at that time when this team existed, when it was set up, the Chief of the General Staff ordered that each collegium meeting should start with a briefing on the part of the operations duty team, but this was not always -- always the case. This was at the time when he requested that this be done by the head. Maps were not used at all times -- well, the maps that were used were those that are always present in the operations centre. As for the slides, I don't recall anything being shown on the slides, but there was discussion about where the units were and what was going on on the basis of the reports that came in during the night or between the two collegium meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, I don't want to show you too many documents, but on the basis of your military experience can you tell me some geographical terms. Where is the Jablanica and Juzni [phoen] Orlovac districts? Are they in Serbia Proper or in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that I could give you a correct answer. I don't know what the administrative divisions were like to tell you where the borders of those districts were. It is in the south, but now whether it was part of the territory of Kosovo or not, I can't really tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. Mr. Dimitrijevic, the next counsel to ask questions will be Mr. Bakrac on behalf of General Lazarevic. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I will be brief. My first question, General, is the following: Do you know that General Lazarevic until January 1998 was in the Nis Corps, that he was the Chief of Staff there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, counsellor. I think he was actually chief of communications there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know that General Lazarevic was transferred into the Pristina Corps in January 1998 on the orders of General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that he was transferred there. I don't know on whose orders, but yes, he was -- he was transferred there, and I think that his post was that of the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in June 1998 - and we have this document, that's 1D760 - at the proposal of General Perisic that General Lazarevic was promoted to a higher rank?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Lazarevic, based on all the evaluations of all of us in the General Staff at the collegium, was an excellent officer, and it was a unanimous decision at the collegium to recommend him for promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Do you know that General Lazarevic from April - that was the time when the forward command post in Djakovica was established - up until the end of that year, that he was actually in Djakovica dealing with the state security -- state border security issues?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that based on my recollection I remember the time when the forward command post was located in Pristina. So as far as I'm concerned, this period begins at a later date. I really didn't register this. I don't recall it being in Djakovica, but I do know that General Lazarevic or Colonel Lazarevic as he was at the time, that he was in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So when we're talking about the forward command post, I'm referring to the forward command post of the Pristina Corps, not of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. Yes, I was thinking about the forward command post of the army. That is why I said that Djakovica, that's not something that I would remember. I know that General Pavkovic sent him to the forward command post. I don't know where it was, but I do know that General Lazarevic was there at the time and that he exercised command and control over activities related to the protection of the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, do you know that General Lazarevic in the performance of his duties was in direct contact and direct communication with the Chief of the General Staff, Mr. Perisic, and that he reported to him about the situation at the state border?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never attended. I was never present when such conversations were made. I assume it was by phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this sounds like General Perisic. He would call his subordinate commanders over the phone and ask them about the situation, whether they needed any assistance, something to be done, yes. So I think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And you have already partially answered this question, but let me ask you what might very well turn out to be my last question. We heard testimony from General Dusan Loncar here, and he said that everybody in the army knew about high professional human qualities of General Lazarevic. A protected witness called by the Prosecution also testified, K-73, also a member --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't need a rehearsal of what other witnesses have said. If you have a question for this witness, please ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This witness, K-73, also stressed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no. Ask this witness his personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Based on your personal knowledge of General Lazarevic, would you say that he was considered as a highly professional soldier, an honest -- an honourable man, a professional commander who defended his country?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that question, please. That was a quite inappropriate question to put as a leading question of that nature after the order I gave you, Mr. Bakrac. Now, if you've something else to turn to, please turn to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well, I don't have anything else, but I was not aware of this stricture, that I was not supposed to ask questions of this nature in the cross-examination. I just wanted the witness to confirm whether what I said was true, and he said he did, but if you think this is inappropriate I don't have any other questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were told not to rehearse the evidence of other witnesses in asking that question, and you proceeded to do it by simply omitting the name of the witnesses. And if you want the Trial Chamber to place any value on character references coming from other witnesses who are familiar with them, you should ask open questions about it. Leading questions about character are useless for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, and indeed, if you had wanted this witness for the purpose of a character witness, it was open for you to have called him as a witness in the trial in the first place. That was not an appropriate use of the time of this witness here at this stage in the trial. Now we'll move to the next and final counsel to cross-examine you, Mr. Dimitrijevic, and that will be Mr. Lukic on behalf of Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, as you've just heard, I know that you're tired but at least there is a light at the end of the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like you to look at Exhibit P1259. Mr. Haider will give you this. You were asked yesterday about page 8 of document P928, about whether you knew about the arming of civilians. We can see a document from the Federal Ministry of Defence, the regional organ in Pristina, the Pristina defence administration. The date is the 21st of May, 1998. Could you please look at item 1 just underneath the word "order." What is ordered here?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it. So that the chiefs of departments and heads of sections shall immediately establish contacts and so on and so forth with municipal leaders and to ensure that lists are compiled for the purpose of arming of the population, which will be carried out by the Ministry of Defence and so on through its organizational units, and the request or demand is made to make sure that those lists should not include persons or conscripts who already have a wartime assignment in units of the army, of the MUP, of the Ministry of Defence, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware that at that time the defence ministry, through its district units, is actually arming the population?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I think that yesterday I spoke about the fact that the army commander ordered, to the best of my recollection, that for the purpose of the defence against any attacks a certain number of persons who were not members of the MUP should get weapons, that weapons should be distributed to them, and that activities followed to put this under control, that all the staffs and branch offices should be mobilised precisely to prevent any misuse of those weapons. As far as I know, there were no such instances. But now I can see that this was going well. I assume that it went down the chain of command, but since the -- those branch organs belonged to the Ministry of Defence organizationally, that is why they are here playing this role. So I think this is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Of course, this relates to the 21st of May, 1999, is that correct, after -- two months after the witness was out of the service?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's 1998, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You can't see the year --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1998. [In English] Maybe it's a mistake in translation, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can't see the date here, but this should be so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us move on, General. Could Mr. Haider show you Exhibit 3D100 next.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 4D100.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, yesterday when you were being asked about the plan: We went to the Grom operation immediately. I don't know whether something remains unclear as regards that. In any case, did you hear of the existence of a global or five-stage plan to counter terrorism; and in relation to that, I will show you two documents.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said yesterday that when President Milosevic ordered that a plan be made, the plan was created by General Pavkovic. Its basis was Grom, which had previously been done on the request of the Supreme Defence Council. Based on that, he devised a plan containing five stages, whereas the earlier plan only had two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this document of the 22nd of July, 1998, we can see that what is envisaged is the participation of the units of MUP and the Pristina Corps. Did you know that the plan envisaged the use of both MUP and Pristina Corps units?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Be so kind as to help me, please. Is this the meeting at which the plan was ordered to be made, or was it one of the subsequent meetings because they were held after each of the stages more or less?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see that a reference is made of the meeting of the 21st of July, 1998, when the implementation was ordered.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR DIMITRIJEVIC [Resumed]
